chapters.title: Introduction — A space to discover
transcript: Welcome to the Church of Santa Margherita, one of the main places to discover religious art in Agira.
Beyond its Neoclassical façade, the interior welcomes visitors with a central nave, two side aisles, a large dome, and a rich collection of sculptures, paintings, and carved woodwork.
Its history spans medieval origins, earthquakes, and rebuilding, alongside centuries of community life.
Let us begin with its origins, before exploring the artworks and details that deserve a closer look.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Between history and tradition
transcript: The medieval layout of Santa Margherita is generally traced to the first half of the thirteenth century.
Local accounts recall an earlier dedication to Saint Sebastian and the possible presence of a Byzantine place of worship dedicated to Saint Sophia.
An even older tradition places a temple of Hercules here, a figure closely associated with the memory of ancient Agira.
It is an evocative story, although a direct connection between that temple and the church has not been established.
The history of Santa Margherita therefore invites us to distinguish documented evidence from traditions passed down over time.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The earthquake and rebuilding
transcript: On the eleventh of January, sixteen ninety-three, a powerful earthquake profoundly affected the building.
According to local historical accounts, the bell tower and the wooden coffered ceiling collapsed.

Rebuilding was a lengthy process, supported in part by contributions from the townspeople. A new roof was followed by the bell tower and work on the transept, the crosswise section of the church, and the apses.
Local sources associate these transformations with Giovanni Battista Vaccarini and Stefano Ittar, leading figures in eighteenth-century Sicilian architecture.
The Neoclassical façade belongs to the nineteenth century.
The church we see today is therefore the result of several periods of construction.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The columns and the dome
transcript: If you can enter, pause for a moment before approaching the altars.
The church has a Latin-cross plan, with fourteen columns separating the central nave from the two side aisles.
Notice the Corinthian capitals, recognisable by their rich decoration of carved leaves.
Then follow the central nave towards the sanctuary, the area around the main altar, before looking up towards the vaults and dome.
The depth of the nave and the upward sweep of the architecture give the interior its distinctive character.
Before examining individual artworks, take in this combination of proportions, light, and space.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Immaculate Virgin by Giuseppe Picano
transcript: Among the church’s principal artworks is the statue of the Immaculate Virgin by the Neapolitan sculptor Giuseppe Picano, created in the late eighteenth century.
The statue stands within a monumental wooden shrine, an architectural structure that frames the figure and emphasises its presence.
This setting was made by Ignazio Leone in eighteen ten.
Notice the movement of the robes, then take a step back to appreciate the whole composition.
The sculpture and its wooden surround are separate works, brought together within the same space.
Here, sculpture and woodcarving combine to create one of the church’s most striking features.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Altars and carved wood
transcript: The seventeenth-century main altar holds a precious detail: miniature decorations in gold on glass.
If you can approach, look closely at the individual decorations and their fine workmanship.

The Altar of the Blessed Sacrament features a small temple-like structure supported by six slender columns. Historical descriptions mention Sicilian marble, Egyptian granite, and agate among its materials.
Woodwork also plays an important role.
The choir stalls are attributed to Giovanni Battista Li Volsi and his son Stefano.
The carved pulpit includes figures of the patron saints of the town’s parishes, connecting its decoration with the religious history of the wider community.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Paintings and memories
transcript: Paintings mentioned in local sources include Mercy, Saint Mary Magdalene, and Our Lady of Sorrows with the Four Evangelists, the last attributed to Ovidio Sozzi.
An eighteenth-century doorway leads into the sacristy, where carved cupboards by Paolo Guglielmazzi of Enna are recorded. Please check with the church before entering this room.
The commemorative inscriptions also tell their stories.
One records the solemn dedication to Saint Margaret on the twentieth of September, eighteen ninety-four.
Another, dated eighteen hundred, commemorates Mauro Manmano e Gussio and the burial place he chose for himself and his family.
Alongside the artworks, these inscriptions preserve the names of people connected with the church.

chapters.title: Closing — Continue exploring
transcript: Our visit to Santa Margherita ends here.
Before leaving, take one last look at the nave, the dome, or a detail that caught your attention.
Please respect the spaces used for prayer and any services taking place. Check with the church about access to its different rooms.
Continue exploring with Hello Agira, a free, independent project created and curated by Giuseppe Ricceri to share and celebrate the town’s heritage.
Thank you for listening, and enjoy discovering Agira!
